Fixing turf on Reunion's fairway-adjacent yards

Turf repair in Reunion, open seams, lifted edges, a melted spot near reflective glass, is quoted per visit as of September 2026 rather than a flat rate, since the fix depends on what's actually wrong. One repair call we get here that's less common elsewhere: turf dented or scuffed by an errant golf shot on a lot backing one of the resort's three fairways.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

Say a stray shot leaves a compressed patch

Say a Reunion homeowner backing the Nicklaus course finds a roughly 8-inch compressed patch in the backyard turf after a ball lands hard during weekend play, along with a seam nearby that's started to peel back about a foot. A repair visit for both issues together, brushing infill back into the compressed spot and re-securing the peeling seam with fresh adhesive, is quoted from photos or a short site visit rather than a fixed menu price, since the seam condition varies more than the golf-ball dent does. Most calls like this get scheduled within the week, faster than a full installation, since the crew is working on an existing base rather than building one from scratch.

Golf-ball impact on fairway-backing lots

A lot that backs any of Reunion's three courses occasionally takes a stray shot into the yard, and turf can show a compressed dent or a scuffed patch where a ball lands hard on a section without much give underneath. That's a narrower, more local repair reason than the seam and edge failures we see everywhere, and fixing it usually means working infill back into the compressed spot and brushing the pile upright rather than replacing the section outright, unless the impact tore the backing.

Choosing the closest pile height when the original is gone

Some turf products get discontinued well before a Reunion lawn reaches the age where it needs a patch, and when that happens the closest available pile height and density, not an exact match, is what a repair actually works with. A slight height difference is easiest to place somewhere it won't draw attention, tucked near a planting bed or under an area furniture usually covers, rather than dead center in an open section of lawn. Being upfront about that tradeoff before the work starts avoids a surprise once the patch is finished and compared against the surrounding turf.

Screen-enclosure edges that work loose

Turf glued along a pool cage's concrete perimeter, common across Reunion's screened lanais, can start to lift at the edge as the adhesive ages or as the concrete itself shifts slightly with seasonal temperature swings. That lifted edge is a different repair than a staked lawn perimeter coming loose in soil, since it calls for re-gluing to a clean, dry slab rather than resetting a stake, and it's worth catching early before foot traffic near the pool works the gap wider.

A capped irrigation head that was never fully removed

Older installs sometimes capped an irrigation head at the surface without pulling the pipe and fitting below it, and that buried hardware can corrode and collapse into a small void over several years, leaving a soft spot that shows up as a dip in the turf above it. On a Reunion property with a lawn more than a decade old, a recurring low spot in roughly the same place a sprinkler zone used to run is worth checking for exactly this before assuming the base simply settled on its own. Digging down to the old fitting and filling the void properly stops the dip from reappearing after each repair.

Reseaming without correcting the water source

A seam that opened because water was standing against it, from a low spot or a grade that never sloped away properly, will reopen again if the repair only reglues the seam without also correcting the grade underneath. On a Reunion lawn, that usually means lifting a wider area than the seam itself, regrading to restore the one to two percent slope, and recompacting before the turf goes back down. Skipping that step to save time on a single visit is the most common reason the same seam generates a second service call within a year.

What a photo can and can't tell us before a visit

A clear, well-lit photo of an open seam or a wrinkle, taken from a few feet back with another shot close up, is usually enough for us to give a Reunion homeowner a preliminary read on scope before scheduling anything. What a photo can't show is the condition of the base underneath, so that first estimate is always a range rather than a firm number, and it can move once someone's actually lifted the turf on site. Sending photos first still saves a visit in the cases where the problem turns out to be smaller than it looked in a phone picture.

Keeping a dog away from a freshly patched dig spot

A repair near a gate or fence line where a dog has been digging needs a short window of managed access on a Reunion property, since the same spot that failed once is exactly where a dog is likely to return to first. A temporary barrier or closer supervision for the day or two while the adhesive fully cures protects the new seam from the one kind of stress, direct digging, that a repair in that location is most at risk from before it's had time to set completely.

Seams that open under rental-home traffic

On a managed rental with steady guest turnover, the seam along a well-worn path, from a patio door to a pool gate, sees more repeated foot traffic than the same seam would in an owner-occupied yard used more lightly, which can open a taped seam faster than it would elsewhere. Reinforcing that specific seam with a stronger adhesive method during a repair visit, rather than just re-taping it the way it was originally done, tends to hold up better against the same traffic pattern going forward.

Questions people ask

Can a golf-ball dent in turf be fixed without replacing the section?

Usually yes, if the backing itself isn't torn. Working infill back into the compressed area and brushing the pile upright resolves most impact dents without cutting out and reseaming a patch.

How fast can a Reunion repair be scheduled?

Faster than a new install in most cases, since there's no base or drainage work involved, though the exact timeline depends on the scope; see the turf repair page for what we look at during a repair visit.
